artwork_title: Remarkable Pieced and Appliqued Cotton Civil War Memorial Quilt
provenance: By family descent, American Furniture & Decorative Arts, Skinner, Boston, Massachusetts, (1 November 2003), Lot 102, to a private Massachusetts collection. | | Literature | This quilt and the family's story is illustrated in Ellen Cort, Wisconsin Quilts: Stories in the Stitches, (Charlottesville: Howell Press, 2001), cover, p. 42-4. | | Note | According to oral family history, the quilt was made by Mary Bell, or Polly as she was known to her friends. In 1854 she married John Shawvan, then began farming in Dodge County. By 1860 they had six children and though John had substantial family obligations, he enlisted, at 34 years of age, into the Union army on 26 October 1861 and was assigned to Company B of the 1st Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry. He was later promoted to the rank of Sergeant and was a color bearer in many battles. Mary assumed full responsibility for the farm, managing the household and caring for the children. During the time he was away she created this quilt for him to share when he returned home. | | In September 1863, Sergeant Shawvan's unit, the 1st Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry, was sent to south Tennessee and participated in the second-bloodiest fight of the entire Civil War, the Battle of Chickamauga. According to Reverend John McNamara, Chaplain of the 1st Wisconsin, "At Chickamauga eighty percent of the regiment was killed, wounded, or taken prisoners. Five officers were killed, five wounded, and three taken prisoners. The color sergeant was killed; the next taking the colors was wounded in three places." Sadly, the color sergeant listed was John Shawvan. He was mortally wounded on the second day of the battle and died on 22 September 1863, at a military hospital in Chattanooga, Tennessee. Polly and the children were left to rely on a Civil War widow's pension.

provenance: Shipped by WridgWays to Melbourne, Australia, 16 December 2001. | | Note | Herts Brothers was a leading interior decorating firm, manufacturing architectural woodwork and "artistic furniture" in New York City from 1872-1937. The marks on this piece date to c. 1872-87, when the company leased warehouse space in Dodworth Hall at 806-8 Broadway, a theater that once adjoined Grace Episcopal Church. The surplus stock at this location, sold without reserve at auction, included "Bedroom Suits in mahogany, cherry, ash, sycamore and walnut, with Armoires, Wardrobes and Chiffoniers to match. Parlor Suits in silk plush, damask, brocatelle and tapestry; conversation and odd shape Chairs; easy Chairs, Lounges, Dining-room Suits in oak and mahogany; Hall Stands, Mirrors, Stained Glass for windows and panels. Mantels in various woods; Easels, Pedestals, together with an assortment of sample pairs of Curtains, Lambrequins, Portieres, &c. in plush, raw silk, satin, velour and cretonne" (New-York Tribune, 26 April 1887). | | Herts counted the Vanderbilts and Astors among their clients, outfitting yachts as well as private homes. The May 1888 issue of Decorator and Furnisher noted that Herts built "the most expensive sideboard ever made in the United States" for the Jim Thorpe, Pennsylvania, dining room of Judge Harry E. Packer, who paid $47,000 for the piece - well over $1.5 million today. In 1891, Steinway & Sons contracted Herts Brothers to furnish their showroom, Steinway Hall, on 14th Street. Herts supplied interior paneling for McKim, Mead & White's New York State Building at the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, where they also exhibited. | | Furniture by Herts Brothers is represented in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Brooklyn Museum, and the Museum of Fine Arts Houston.

provenance: By extra-lineal descent to consignor from Robert Crighton (1821-82), Port Glasgow, Scotland. | | Literature | The gold medal and box illustrated in Clare Abbott, Faithful of Days: The Story of Robert Crighton, Master Mariner (Oxford: Youcaxton, 2014), fig. 11, 15. | | Lot Essay | | Robert Crighton left Scotland an obscure merchant mariner and returned six months later an American hero. On 24 November 1853, the Captain of Three Bells departed Glasgow with a crew of twenty-four, sixteen passengers, and a cargo of brandy, textiles, and iron. She crawled into New York harbor two months later with 185 people rescued from the steamship San Francisco. That ship, chartered by the U.S. Army to carry the 13th Artillery regiment to California, had been sighted in disabled condition almost three weeks earlier. Nine vessels and a sloop-of-war had embarked from Boston to Charleston in search of her, but it was Three Bells of Glasgow that broke news of her sad fate. | | When Crighton spotted her distress signals on New Year's Eve 1853, San Francisco had been "rolling about mastless and rudderless, a huge log upon the ocean" for seven days. On the second day of her maiden voyage, the steamer rode into the worst hurricane of the century. Overnight, violent waves "stripped the starboard paddle box, carried away starboard after right-post, both smokestacks, all the upper saloon, staving the quarter-deck through, and washing overboard [about 140] passengers," who invariably drowned. Then the engine failed. As the storm continued to rage, stranded passengers saw two ships come and go, one making off with their jettisoned provisions. Another ship, Kilby, boarded 100 people - including the regiment's commander - before the hawsers snapped and waves drove the vessels apart. Dozens of people - including a family of four - had died of cholera. | | Crighton is credited with sending the desperate people the message "Be of good cheer, I will not desert you" using chalkboards because oral communication was impossible over the din. He kept his word. Three Bells rode out the storm at her side for three days. By January 5th, the weather calm and the ship Antarctic now drawn into the lifesaving mission, over 300 people were rescued from the wreckage, the last being Captain J.T. Watkins of the San Francisco, who scuttled her. The Antarctic continued to Liverpool, where she landed all 220 survivors. | | 223 people boarded Three Bells, but more than thirty died of disease on board; 185 survivors were reported upon her arrival in New York. As Crighton's biographer Clare Abbott notes, "185 is still a large number ... down six generations since 1854, there could today be over ten thousand people who owe their existence to Robert Crighton" (Faithful of Days, p. 48). | | | Private subscriptions to recognize the many sailors participating in the rescue were soon established across the country. An estimated $84,470 was raised by committees in New York, Boston, Philadelphia, Baltimore, and San Francisco - about $10,000 of this intended for Crighton himself. The contemporary press offered detailed descriptions of the additional gifts of gold and silver commissioned for the Captains, including the three testimonials comprising the present lot: | | On January 27th, the gold box was presented to Crighton with the Freedom of the City of New York during a ceremony at the Astor House Hotel, followed by a reception with Governor Horatio Seymour, U.S. General Winfield Scott, and over 2,000 cheering spectators. Later, confronted by missing payment records for the gold snuff box, whose origin is unknown, Alderman Orison Blunt of the Common Council confessed to buying it himself, for fear that "the occasion might not be sufficiently splendid" (Faithful of Days, p. 66). | | The gold medal from the Merchants & Citizens of New York, procured from Ball, Black & Co., was first displayed at the New York Exchange in March 1855. | | And the coin silver salver, commissioned by members of the Boston Merchant's Exchange, was on view at Jones, Ball & Co. in Boston by January 28th and likely traveled with Crighton on his (not uneventful) return journey to Scotland that April. The salver is remarkably similar to one without an inscription that Jones, Ball & Co. displayed at the New York Crystal Palace Exhibition a few months earlier, illustrated in Gleason's Pictorial Drawing-Room Companion 5/10 (3 September 1853): 153. | | Given the overwhelming U.S. military presence on board San Francisco, local commissions urged the federal government to follow their example. Congress approved funding for gold lifesaving medals in July 1866, twelve years after the disaster. Crighton finally received his Congressional Gold Medal of Honor in 1869, while docked in Norfolk, Virginia, as Captain of the merchant ship Venezuelan. He is among the few foreign nationals to receive the prize. Its location today is unknown. | | | Tributes also abounded in popular culture. While in New York, Crighton sat for a portrait at Mathew Brady's daguerreotype studio on Broadway. The original is lost, but the Captain's likeness survives on sheet music for such hit songs as The Three Bells Quickstep; The Wreck of the San Francisco; Be Cheery Boys, be Cheery; The Three Bells Polka and its sequel, The Four Bells Polka. | | A painting of the rescue "by F.H. Lane of Boston," in a frame inscribed "Presented to Capt. Robert Crighton, by the merchants of Boston," was exhibited in New York in the summer of 1854, but is otherwise unrecorded. No artist has been identified for the poignant scene on the Ball, Black & Co. gold medals, and it is tempting to consider that Lane's lost painting was the source. Nathaniel Currier issued a colored lithograph of the rescue, titled The San Francisco Tragedy, the same year. | | Two decades later, John Greenleaf Whittier published his poem "The Three Bells" in The Atlantic Monthly with the preface: "Many readers will remember Captain Leighton of the English ship Three Bells, who some years ago rescued the crew of an American vessel sinking in mid-ocean." Such inaccuracies did not likely offend Crighton, whose name is misspelled "Creighton" on the New York medal as well as his Congressional Medal of Honor. He did not seek the riches lavishly bestowed upon him by grateful Americans. His primary concern after landing was the financial toll of his heroism on the owners of Three Bells and her cargo. To the end of his life, Crighton maintained the simple view professed in his acceptance of a gold box from Alderman Blunt: "I have performed nothing more than a humanitary duty — a duty which I feel that any man, animated by the common sympathies of human nature, would gladly have done under similar circumstances." Alderman Blunt surmised at the time that Crighton, if not exactly by name, would be "revered by coming generations, when every being who beholds the sun of this day shall be a tenant of the tomb." | | Identified simply as "the skipper," Crighton and his rare strength of character shine brightest in Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass (1855): | | "I understand the large hearts of heroes, | The courage of present times and all times, | How the skipper saw the crowded and rudderless wreck of the steam-ship, and Death chasing it up and down the storm, | How he knuckled tight and gave not back an inch, and was faithful of days and faithful of nights, | And chalk'd in large letters on a board, Be of good cheer, we will not desert you; | How he follow'd with them and tack'd with them three days and would not give it up, | How he saved the drifting company at last, | How the lank loose-gown'd women look'd when boated from the side of their prepared graves, | How the silent old-faced infants and the lifted sick, and the sharp-lipp'd unshaved men; | All this I swallow, it tastes good, I like it well, it becomes mine, | I am the man, I suffer'd, I was there."

description_block: Artist Name: Memorial to Francis and Polly Gray  | Artwork Title: signed Frances Gray (age 8), Boston, Massachusetts, 1801 | Lot Info: None | signed Frances Gray (age 8), Boston, Massachusetts, 1801 watercolor and silk embroidery on silk panel 16 1/2 x 22 in. framed 18 3/4 x 24 1/4 in. Francis Gray (c. 1748-95) was a Boston merchant who married Mary "Polly" Young (c. 1762-97) in 1785. The maker, Frances Gray (born c. 1793), was likely their orphaned daughter, who would have completed this memorial picture as part of her school education. Teachers and hired artists would trace designs from engraved prints in ink and watercolor on woven textiles for students to embellish with silk embroidery threads. A similar monument surmounted by an angel appears in an 1803 needlework from the female academy of Mrs. Saunders and Miss Beach in Dorchester, Massachusetts, whose 1500-volume library included "the finest patterns for Drawing in Figures, Landscapes, Fruit, Flowers &c." according to advertisements. The composition is overwhelmingly derived from Classical European sources, themselves indebted to ancient Egypt for the funereal symbolism of pyramids and obelisks, which became highly popular in the United States during the period of national mourning for George Washington (d. 1799). The single mourning woman in Frances' embroidery closely resembles an allegorical figure of "America in Tears" at Washington's tomb, reproduced in countless prints. More local in character is the church on the far right, whose mighty tower displays a New England staple: the Atlantic Codfish. Information about Frances is scarce; her identity is largely inferred from historical records of her parents, as well as by the fortuitous survival of recycled paper on the reverse, printed for Boston dry goods merchants Churchill & Watson.

provenance: Joseph Thomas (1791-1835) and Christiana Rittenour Thomas (1788-1867) of Frederick County, Virginia, and Greene County, Ohio. | Their daughter, Sophronia Thomas Carr (1813-97) of Fayette and Greene County. | Her son Thaddeus Plato Carr (1850-1920) and daughter-in-law Elizabeth Brewster Botsford (1849-1919) of Greene County. | Their daughter Harriet Botsford Carr Neibel (1879-1937) of St. Paul, Minnesota. | Her daughter Dorothy Elizabeth Neibel Whitson (1909-2008) of St. Paul; painting in her possession by 1957. | Thence by descent to consignor. | | | Note | The itinerant preacher Joseph Thomas, self-styled and later immortalized in American folklore as The White Pilgrim, left his North Carolina home at age 16 to join an informal network of Christian evangelists leading the Second Great Awakening in the United States. Eschewing all denominations, Thomas modeled himself after Lorenzo Dow, particularly in his publication of a memoir, which relates his often-harrowing experiences preaching only the Scripture along the backroads of Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Kentucky, and Ohio. His wife and children were settled in Yellow Springs, Ohio, when Thomas caught smallpox in New York City, where he was meeting with the editors of the Christian Palladium. He died soon afterwards at the home of a colleague in Johnsonburg, New Jersey. Fear of the disease spreading, exacerbated by Thomas' status as a stranger in town, all the stranger for being dressed entirely in white, led to his burial in an unmarked grave opposite the Dark Moon tavern. | | Visiting the site around 1838, Elder John Ellis wrote an elegy - beginning "I came to the spot where / The white pilgrim lay / And pensively stood by the tomb" - that became a popular hymn set to the tune of Lily Dale, and was often sung at funerals. The expanded verse, which addresses the White Pilgrim's widow and children, would be frequently invoked to lament the death of someone far from home. Indeed, the identity of the White Pilgrim as Joseph Thomas was soon forgotten, and the song would be subtitled "The Missionary Who Died in Africa" or "Supposed to be Written by an Indian" in the press. An excellent report on its origins and reiterations is given in D.K. Wilgus, "'The White Pilgrim' Song, Legend, and Fact," Southern Folklore Quarterly 14/3 (September 1950): 177-84. Bob Dylan recorded a version of the song for his 1993 album World Gone Wrong.

description_block: Artist Name: Book and Manuscript Collection of The White Pilgrim | Artwork Title:  Joseph Thomas (1791-1835), 1810 and later | Lot Info: None | Joseph Thomas (1791-1835), 1810 and later Unique library and manuscript collection descended in the family of Rev. Joseph Thomas, an evangelical Christian preacher, poet, and hymn writer, who inspired the traditional song "The White Pilgrim" (or "The Lone Pilgrim"), as well as folklore and ghost stories from Johnsonburg, New Jersey, to the Ohio frontier. Eighteen books published between 1810 and 1870 include Thomas' personal copies of his own Pilgrim's Hymn Book (1816) and Life of the Pilgrim, Joseph Thomas (1817) published in Winchester, Virginia, by Jonathan Foster; two volumes of William Cowper's Poems (1814) inscribed "Joseph Thomas 1817" on the page edges; James Montgomery's Greenland, and other poems (1819) "Bot of Joseph Gates in Raleigh, No Carolina, July 2nd 1821"; and Edward Young's Night Thoughts on Life, Death and Immortality (1810) "bot at White Post March 22nd 1816 – Frederick Co. Va. Price 50 cents". Collection of correspondence and genealogical notes spans five generations. Three letters from Joseph to his wife Christiana Rittenour Thomas, two signed "Joseph Thomas Pilgrim" and one with the signature excised, describe what would prove to be his last preaching circuit, through New York and New Jersey, in 1835. In another two letters to Christiana, Thomas' colleague Elder Isaac Newton Walter - the "Pioneer Preacher of Ohio" and a founder of the Disciples of God Christian Church - had the burden of recounting her husband's sudden death from smallpox and his hasty burial on the outskirts of Warren County, New Jersey. Sold together with a circa 1950 oil on canvas copy of the March 1835 portrait taken in New York City by William Hillyer, Jr. (1815-1904), mere weeks before Thomas' death. Isaac Walter refers to the portrait in his letters to Christiana, stating that it was a gift from the artist to be sent from New Jersey along with Thomas' personal effects. Hillyer's portrait was likely the model for a wood engraving in the 1861 Christian Messenger edition of The life, travels, and gospel labors of Eld. Joseph Thomas . The copy is mounted on plywood board and framed, "Painted by Wm Hillyer / March 1835" inscribed on the whitewashed reverse, framed 33 1/8 x 25 1/2 in.

provenance: Estate of Daniel Meyer Friedenberg (1923-2011), Curator Emeritus of Coins and Medals at the Jewish Museum, New York, New York. | New England Auction Company, Danbury, Connecticut (20 November 2011), Lot 11. | | Note | Alexander Agassiz (1835-1910) was born in Switzerland, the son of prominent natural scientist Louis Agassiz (1807-73). In 1849, he joined his father in the United States, where the elder Agassiz served as a professor of zoology and geology at Harvard University. Alexander received two degrees from Harvard and supported his father's work at the University's Museum of Comparative Zoology. Elected to the American Academy of Arts & Sciences in 1862, Alexander went on to serve as the President of that society from 1894-1903. His most significant contributions to geology and engineering were as a managing investor in the Calumet and Hecla Mining Company, which became a leading supplier in the global market for copper by the 1870s. This commemorative plaque, based on a carte-de-visite taken circa 1900, was cast shortly after Agassiz's death on board the RMS Adriatic in 1910. A slightly smaller version is in the collection of Harvard Art Museums (acc. no. B33), and a reduced scale medal is in the Yale University Art Gallery (acc. no. 2013.86.33), where the artist Bela Lyon Pratt received his B.F.A. in 1899.
